summary: Escape Velocity is a free, browser-based retro 3D game in which kids aged 7 to 12 run a base on Mars (or the Moon) across three generations of crews. The same machine that makes air to breathe also makes oxygen for the rocket home, so every power cell spent on heat, food, a radiation shelter or building the base is a cell not filling the tank: no choice is free, and our automated tests prove it. Real NASA data drives the game: solar storms are actual flares and eruptions from NASA's DONKI database, fetched live and labeled LIVE or ARCHIVE; message delays come from JPL orbit data; and the terrain and landing sites come from NASA Mars Trek and SWIM ice maps. Each crew inherits the base the last one built, so students learn to plan for the people who come after them. Rival races, rover expeditions, a base designer and a free season pass keep kids coming back, and class codes, a live teacher dashboard, team rooms and a teacher guide turn it into a complete, free lesson.
details:
We built a campaign game where every decision costs something, and the base a crew builds outlives the crew.

Play it: https://playescapevelocity.com (no download, no login). Teacher guide: https://playescapevelocity.com/teacher/. Code: https://github.com/swimmer-303/escape-velocity.

What it does. A campaign follows three crews of 4, 5 and 6 astronauts to the same base in Gale Crater. Each sol (Mars day), players place a limited number of power cells on the O2 plant (air to breathe or oxygen for the rocket), the greenhouse, heaters, a storm shelter, and once built, a radiation monitor and a battery. Spare cells go to the Workshop, which builds upgrades every later crew keeps: solar panels, a regolith berm, a bigger O2 plant, a fission reactor and more. Each crew must fill its rocket before the launch window closes. Then the base waits 26 months for the next crew (the real gap between Earth-Mars launch windows) while the O2 plant pre-fills the next rocket.

How it works. Each sol has four steps:

  1. Morning briefing: weather, power, and Earth's space-weather forecast, delayed by today's real Earth-Mars light time (about 11 minutes).
  2. Budget: drag or tap cells onto modules. Ghost bars preview the result before you commit, and "Suggest a plan" gives first-time players a starting plan with a reason for each choice.
  3. Run: the 3D outpost plays the day out, from sunrise to a blue Mars sunset to night.
  4. Debrief: one plain sentence of cause and effect, plus a Real Science card.

Under the hood, a deterministic, seeded simulation (TypeScript) turns real DONKI events into each mission's storms. X-class storms send the fastest particles, so they can beat Earth's warning to Mars; a local radiation monitor is the fix, as in real Mars planning. More than 360 automated tests prove that moving any useful power cell to another job always makes something worse, that careful play wins, and that pure greed always loses. The browser gets space weather from our server, which caches NASA DONKI for an hour; if NASA is unreachable, a stored snapshot is used and labeled ARCHIVE, never LIVE.

More ways to play and teach. Players can land at Gale Crater, at ice-rich Arcadia Planitia (from NASA's SWIM ice maps), or on the Moon (1.3-second messages, about twice the radiation, a long lunar night, oxygen from soil). Replay History puts the real solar storms of May 2024 on their real dates. A space weather radar shows the last 30 days of real eruptions crossing the solar system next to NASA's own ENLIL predictions, and a trip planner solves the real orbital problem (Lambert's problem) to draw a porkchop plot of every launch date and flight time from Mars back to Earth, showing why crews can only leave every 26 months. Teachers get class codes (the same Mars for the whole class), a live dashboard of every crew's results, and Mission Control team rooms where students share one power budget from their own devices. A daily challenge gives everyone the same real-Sun mission, with a leaderboard the server verifies by replaying each game.

Built to keep kids playing for hours, and learning the whole time. Everything rewards playing well: sheltering the crew, building for the next one, launching on time. An Astronaut Rank gives XP for every sol, storm survived, upgrade built and rocket launched, with 50 levels, 11 ranks and something new unlocked at almost every level. Three daily missions give everyone the same small goals each day. Storm Cards turn every real NASA solar storm a crew faces into a collectible card, with rarity taken from the real flare class (C common, M rare, X epic, X5 and up legendary) and a link to its NASA DONKI record; because the feed is live, new cards appear as the real Sun erupts. The Hangar unlocks suit colors, rocket paint, base lights and a rover pet that show up in the 3D outpost. Two flight mini-games add action: land the crew under real Mars or Moon gravity, and fly the rocket to escape velocity, with medals for skill and never a penalty for the mission. Nothing is bought, there are no ads, and progress stays on the player's device.

New for the final build: four more ways to play, and a new 3D look. Rival Race: race three computer rival commanders on the same base with the same real storms, through leagues from Bronze to Legend, with live standings and a podium; send a friend a challenge link and they race your recorded run (no account, no server). Rover Expeditions: drive a rover across the real ground around your base (Gale Crater or Arcadia Planitia, from NASA Mars Trek heights) or near the Moon's south pole, collect 5 to 8 science targets a day into a Sample Museum, and manage the battery, because no choice is free. Outpost Architect: design a Mars or Moon base on a grid with a live readout of power, air, food, heat and storm safety from the game's own numbers, then stress-test it against a real NASA solar storm across 12 Blueprint challenges. Solar Season: a free 40-tier season pass with weekly challenges and Live Sun Events from NASA DONKI (labeled ARCHIVE when the data is not live), earned only by playing. New 3D: blue Martian sunsets, dust storms that darken the sky, Phobos and Deimos at night, glowing base lights, and Earth low over the Moon's south pole with long shadows; slower school laptops automatically get a lighter version. Demo video: https://youtu.be/usbovDr12Ew. Pitch slides: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/e/2PACX-1vR1zBcMjuSCcGlrC5OLeNFsK-heXtk5rzGBrbvgh5AOQxN4r7W5drXkGSW0wI8itH_82Y_LXuA0ehBL/pub

Settings and the Space Lab. A Settings screen lets players switch music and sound effects on or off separately, each with its own volume slider, and choose reduced motion, 3D detail (Auto, Faster for slow Chromebooks, or Sharper), larger text, high contrast, dyslexia-friendly spacing and read-aloud. The Space Lab is a what-if science lab built as a fair test: players change one real factor at a time and watch what it does to their base, with live readouts and the 3D scene reacting. Its six dials are the world (Gale Crater, Arcadia Planitia or the Moon's south pole), Sun activity (solar minimum to maximum, still dealing only real NASA DONKI storms), Mars in its orbit (about 45% more sunlight at the closest point, by the inverse-square law and NASA's Mars Fact Sheet, but that is dust storm season), dust in the air (up to tau 10.8, the 2018 planet-wide storm that ended NASA's Opportunity rover), the message delay from Earth (3 to 22 light-minutes; about 1.3 seconds on the Moon) and crew size (about 0.9 kg of oxygen per person per day, from NASA's BVAD). Kids write down a hypothesis, fly the same storms again, and get a result card that compares real and lab conditions and explains the science, and a Lab Notebook keeps their experiments. It is the game's own model with real numbers, not a NASA simulation, and lab missions never count for leaderboards, races or the season, so the competitive modes stay fair.

Benefits.

  • Students feel real engineering trade-offs and long-term planning, not just read about them.
  • Real data literacy: every storm card names the real event and links to its NASA record; the in-game Science Log shows every source and every simplification.
  • Failure teaches without punishing: a crew that runs short heads home early, the game says why and what to try, and the base carries on.
  • Built for classrooms: no login or download, runs on Chromebooks, saves after every sol, a one-minute guided first sol, and a teacher guide with a 45 to 55 minute lesson plan, NGSS links (3-5-ETS1, MS-ETS1, MS-ESS1), discussion questions and a worksheet.
  • Accessible: mouse, touch and keyboard; read-aloud for early readers; larger text, high contrast and dyslexia-friendly spacing; reduced motion; every meter has an icon, a label and a number, never color alone.
  • Private: no accounts, no ads, no names or emails collected.

From Mars to Earth: better lives and a healthier planet. A Mars base runs on the same ideas that conserve resources on Earth: a strict energy budget, stored solar power, recycled water, and food grown with less. At the end of every mission, the game links what the crew did to NASA technology already helping people here, each with its NASA Spinoff source: space-station water recycling that led to water-saving showers and village water filters, NASA's first vertical farm and today's indoor farms, and NASA-invented flow batteries that store solar power for community microgrids.

What we simplified. Time is compressed (one sol plays in about 30 seconds), fuel amounts are scaled down, and the radiation budget is far stricter than NASA's real 600 mSv career limit, so radiation choices matter in a short game. The in-game Science Log lists every simplification and all of our 70+ sources; the NASA Data list below has room for the main 25.

Tools and languages. TypeScript, Vite and Three.js (WebGL) for a PlayStation-1-style retro 3D outpost that runs fast on school Chromebooks; Vitest and happy-dom for tests; Node.js and Caddy on a DigitalOcean server, with GitHub Actions running every test before each automatic deploy; Python for art processing.

Use of AI. The code was written with AI assistance (Claude Code by Anthropic) from our design brief: we set the concept and rules, checked the science, play-tested, and asked for changes. All 13 illustrations and the crew portraits were generated with Higgsfield (GPT Image 2.6), and the 3 music tracks with Higgsfield (ElevenLabs Music v2.5). The logo was made with Claude (Anthropic). As the Space Apps organizer confirmed, we disclose this once rather than watermarking each image: at the bottom of the game's title screen, on the first slide, in the in-game Credits, in an ai-assistance meta tag, in the README, and in ASSETS.md with every prompt. All data comes from NASA sources, not AI, and no NASA logos, flags, mission patches or insignia appear in any asset.
